messages.body_plain:
Hi Hend,

Depending on what method you used with fscores, the estimates should should be around the mean of the latent variable (which by default is 0 for each latent trait). The values won't be exactly equal to 0 in any particular method simply because of the estimation algorithms, but in general you can't compare the means of the trait across estimates because they are all approximately equal to 0 in the population. So any numerical differences are really meaningless and not at all an issue. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: X2 statistics in mirt
messages.body_plain:
This can happen with the MHRM algorithm because it is stochastic, so parameters are only approximations of the true ML estimates. However, note that these models are not nested, so you can't really use a X2 test anyway. Use the information criteria like AIC and BIC to inform your modeling decision (in this case the UIRT model fits about as well as the MIRT, so nothing is really gained). You could also compare goodness of fit with M2() to see if there is any modeling improvements, but I doubt it given how close these models match the data.

Phil

Just as a follow up, this is what ltm is doing but with mirt's functions:

library(ltm)
library(mirt)
dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)

Model <- ltm(dat ~ z1)

plot(Model, type = "IIC", items = 0, lwd = 2, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.main = 1.3)
info <- information(Model, c(-3, 0))

                                    "\n\nInformation in (-3, 0):", round(info$InfoRange, 3),
                                    paste("(", round(100 * info$PropRange, 2), "%)", sep = "")), cex = 1.2)

mod <- mirt(dat, 1)
f <- function(theta, mod) testinfo(mod, matrix(theta))
(ii <- integrate(f, lower = -3, upper = 0, mod=mod))
(iT <- integrate(f, lower = -10, upper = 10, mod=mod))

Theta <- matrix(seq(-3,3, length.out=1000))
info <- testinfo(mod, Theta)
plot(info ~ Theta, type = 'l')
text(x = 2, y = 0.5, labels = paste("Total Information:", round(iT$value, 3),
                                    "\n\nInformation in (-3, 0):", round(ii$value, 3),
                                    paste("(", round(100 * ii$value/iT$value, 2), "%)", sep = "")), cex = 1.2)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Katherine,

This looks to be legacy documentation because I removed this option a while back. Sorry for not fixing the help files accordingly.

To use simdata you should convert your standardized loadings manually to slopes (see Wirth & Edwards 2007 for more details). Below is some example code. Cheers.

# convert factor loadings to slopes
F2a <- function(F, D=1.702){
    h2 <- rowSums(F^2)
    a <- (F / sqrt(1 - h2)) * D
    a
}

(F <- matrix(c(rep(.7, 5), rep(.5,5))))
(a <- lambda2a(F))
d <- rnorm(10)

dat <- simdata(a, d, 5000, itemtype = 'dich')
mod <- mirt(dat, 1)
coef(mod, simplify=TRUE)
summary(mod)

Phil

Hi Phil,
    Interesting and thanks for your expanded answer on the mirt and ltm crossover. The reason for quantifying the area under the curve is for Polytomous items in psychological scale construction. As the discrimination parameter is less useful here, I want to be able to compare similar items and groups. To do this, it is useful to be able to compare the amount of information between very similar combinations of items to determine optimum scale construction. quantifying the information seems like a better way that visually comparing very similar IIC/SIC and would also allow us to look quantify where the information lies: e.g., item one has 80% of information between -1 and 1 logits and thus is targeted at this population.  For our purposes, it would also be useful to be able to overlap the information curves for all the items within the scale to compare them directly.

Seongho is probably right that the best strategy is to simply collapse categories, or perhaps not use the rating scale models at all (they rarely fit well anyway).

That being said, you can hack at some of the code by including survey weights for arbitrary response patterns to trick the program into thinking that categories exist when they really don't. This might have unforeseen consequences in secondary functions, but for model comparison reasons it's fine. See below.

library(mirt)

dat <- Science
dat[,2] <- dat[,2] + 1
dat[,3] <- dat[,3] + 2
dat[,4] <- dat[,4] + 2
lapply(dat, table)

dummy <- matrix(min(dat):max(dat), nrow=6, ncol=4)
colnames(dummy) <- colnames(dat)

w <- c(rep(0, 6), rep(1, nrow(dat)))
mod <- mirt(rbind(dummy, dat), 1, 'grsmIRT', survey.weights = w)
coef(mod, simplify=TRUE)

plot(mod, type = 'trace')

itemfit(mod)
personfit(mod)
fscores(mod)

Phil

messages.subject: Re: longitudinal Rasch model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lina,

What you are describing sounds more like a multiple-group type question than a longitudinal model. For latent longitudinal models to work you generally have to have a stronger type of invariance assumed in order to properly equate the time points (e.g., the intercept in the first item wave 1 must be equal to the first intercept wave 2 and 3, so that changes can be expressed in terms of population mean differences; same type of reasoning for latent growth curves). Rasch models are a bit easier because the slopes are already constrained to be equal by default, so this makes them rather appealing if they turn out to be suitable for the data. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Some Observations on multipleGroup output in vertical equating
messages.body_plain: Hi All: When one has multiple groups with some overlapping items as in 2 stage testing or irt vertical equating, the command 'coef(result,IRTpars=TRUE,simplify=TRUE) does not give one the traditional IRT parameters and you have to rescale the 'a' parameter by dividing by 1.7. When subjects take 20 or more items in the two stage testing situation (vertical equating), the default extimation procedures yield results that nicely replicate those of commercial software such as bilog-mg with the above rescaling.  In the neighborhood of 15 items, default estimation is quite a bit off from bilog-mg, but if one does MHRM the estimates  become much closer.  This is not surprising since bilog-mg uses EM followed by Newon-Raphson. In a 9 item example with 3 unique items in each of two groups and thus 3 common items, multipleGroup yields some "off-the wall" estimates while bilog-mg yields seemingly reasonable estimates for this admittedly minimum information example.  Now bilog-mg does have default priors but it is hard to replicate them in the multipleGroup except possibly for the 'a' parameter. One other observation, command 'summary' does not seem to work for MHRM estimation. All of these examples are one dimensional dichotomous items.Cheers Don Rock

messages.body_plain:
Hi Don,

Sounds like some interesting observations, some of which sound a little peculiar since I wouldn't expect bilog to provide results that are so discrepant (I have used multipleGroup pretty extensively, and it provides results that I would expect). Could you provide something that I could reproduce to see these issues, perhaps generated with the simdata() function and analysed with bilog/mirt to obtain the suitable text output files? Cheers.

Phil

On Mon, Feb 29, 2016 at 11:02 AM, 'Donald Rock' via mirt-package <mirt-p...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> Hi All: When one has multiple groups with some overlapping items as in 2 stage testing or irt vertical equating, the command 'coef(result,IRTpars=TRUE,simplify=TRUE) does not give one the traditional IRT parameters and you have to rescale the 'a' parameter by dividing by 1.7. When subjects take 20 or more items in the two stage testing situation (vertical equating), the default extimation procedures yield results that nicely replicate those of commercial software such as bilog-mg with the above rescaling.  In the neighborhood of 15 items, default estimation is quite a bit off from bilog-mg, but if one does MHRM the estimates  become much closer.  This is not surprising since bilog-mg uses EM followed by Newon-Raphson. In a 9 item example with 3 unique items in each of two groups and thus 3 common items, multipleGroup yields some "off-the wall" estimates while bilog-mg yields seemingly reasonable estimates for this admittedly minimum information example.  Now bilog-mg does have default priors but it is hard to replicate them in the multipleGroup except possibly for the 'a' parameter. One other observation, command 'summary' does not seem to work for MHRM estimation. All of these examples are one dimensional dichotomous items.Cheers Don Rock

For example my 1st Item is Score in math and 2nd is score in engineering and 3rd item is developing software. I wish to see how the latent trait in math affect the latent trait in engineering. I have a longitudinal model, where my goal is to see how the latent trait in math over time affects the latent trait in engineering. The 3rd item is developing software. My goal in the next step is to see how the latent trait in math and engineering in combination affects the latent trait in developing software. My idea was to use multidimensional IRT to achieve this. If there is any other way, I shall be glad to learn about it. I highly appreciate any suggestion on this.

Thanks
Souvik
